The source was not yet obtained before; it is now downloaded and the quotation is confirmed verbatim on p.13. sources.note: Modern Haroi has a restructured register system: initials > phonation (voice-quality) register > vowel registers > loss of voice-quality distinctions, leaving a large unconditioned vowel inventory; pre-Haroi register = breathy vowels after voiced obstruents vs modal elsewhere; Table 1 'Restructured register and Haroi vowel splitting' (tense / modal / breathy voice); correlates the changes with Smith's 1972 Proto-North-Bahnaric. No contrastive tone described for modern Haroi.

tone.quote: Modern Haroi has what Huffman (1976) termed a restructured register system. In the case of Haroi, between PC and modern Haroi the following chain of events has occurred: (1) certain classes of initials led to distinctive phonation differences on the following vowels, that is, a register system with voice quality differences; (2) the voice quality differences on the vowels produced vowel distinctions, that is, led to a register system with vowel registers; and, (3) the voice quality distinctions that originally conditioned the vowel splits disappeared, leaving behind a large number of now unconditioned vowel distinctions;

sources.citation: Thurgood, Graham. 1997. Restructured Register in Haroi: Reconstructing its Historical Origins. In Abramson, Arthur S. (ed.), Southeast Asian Linguistic Studies in Honour of Vichin Panupong, 283-296. Bangkok: Chulalongkorn University Press.
sources.note: First-hand historical-phonological account of Haroi prosody/phonation: modern Haroi is a 'restructured register system' (Huffman 1976) - earlier phonation (register) distinctions conditioned vowel splits and were then lost, leaving c. 32 contrasting main-syllable vowels; no contrastive tone or phonation is described for the modern language; also states all monosyllables are tonic (stressed) and disyllables are pretonic presyllable + tonic main syllable. Reconstructs an earlier three-way phonation distinction.

tone.quote: Modern Haroi has what Huffman (1976) termed a restructured register system. [...] At this point Haroi had developed into a register language: that is, it had two (or more) sets of vowels distinguished by phonation type. If the vowels did not do so immediately, these vowel registers came to differ not only in phonation type, but also in vowel quality. Then, with the loss of the phonation type differences, the originally predictable vowel quality differences became phonemic—Haroi was now a restructured register system.

sources.note: 'The Chamic languages of Vietnam have undergone phonological restructuring..' - in contact with Mon-Khmer all developed final stress; Western Cham developed register, Phan Rang Cham incipient tones, Tsat full tones, and Haroi (in contact with Bahnar/Hrê) a restructured register realised as vowel-quality splits rather than pitch. Likely the fullest journal treatment of why Haroi has vowel registers instead of tones.
